description: Descriptive statistics, random number and variate generation, symbolic probability distributions, and inference. Distributions are symbolic objects that work with PDF, CDF, Mean, Variance, Expectation and RandomVariate uniformly, so the same code works for parametric, derived, empirical and transformed distributions.

tools.name: Mean
tools.description: Gives the arithmetic mean of a list, of the columns of a matrix, or of a symbolic probability distribution. For a matrix it returns the vector of column means. Applied to a distribution it gives the exact symbolic expectation, which is how the same function serves both data and theory.
tools.example:
Mean[{1, 2, 3, 4}]
Mean[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}]
Mean[NormalDistribution[mu, sigma]]
Mean[N[data]]
Mean[Quantity[{1, 2, 3}, "Meters"]]
tools.notes: Related location measures include Median, Commonest, GeometricMean, HarmonicMean, TrimmedMean and WinsorizedMean for robust alternatives.

tools.name: Median
tools.description: Gives the median of a list or the median of a distribution, averaging the two middle values for an even-length list. It is the robust location measure, unaffected by extreme outliers. For a matrix it returns the column-wise medians.
tools.example:
Median[{1, 2, 3, 100}]
Mean[{1, 2, 3, 100}]
Median[NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
Median[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 6}}]

tools.name: Commonest
tools.description: Gives the list of most frequently occurring elements, which is the statistical mode, returning several values when there is a tie. Commonest[list, n] gives the n most common values in order of frequency. It works on any elements, not just numbers.
tools.example:
Commonest[{1, 2, 2, 3, 3}]
Commonest[{a, b, a, c, a}]
Commonest[RandomInteger[5, 100], 3]
First[Commonest[words]]
tools.notes: The result is always a list even when there is a unique mode; wrap in First when a single value is expected. Counts gives the full frequency table.

tools.name: Variance
tools.description: Gives the unbiased sample variance of a list, dividing by n-1, or the exact variance of a distribution. For a matrix it returns the variance of each column. Use it with StandardDeviation for spread and with Covariance for relationships between variables.
tools.example:
Variance[{1, 2, 3, 4}]
Variance[NormalDistribution[mu, sigma]]
Variance[{{1, 2}, {3, 4}, {5, 7}}]
Variance[RandomVariate[PoissonDistribution[3], 1000]]
tools.notes: Wolfram Language uses the n-1 (unbiased) divisor for lists; multiply by (n-1)/n to get the population variance.

tools.name: StandardDeviation
tools.description: Gives the square root of the sample variance for a list, or the exact standard deviation of a distribution. It is the most common measure of spread and shares the units of the data. For a matrix it acts column by column.
tools.example:
StandardDeviation[{1, 2, 3, 4}]
StandardDeviation[NormalDistribution[0, sigma]]
StandardDeviation[data]/Sqrt[Length[data]]
Standardize[data]
tools.notes: Standardize[data] subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation in one step, which is the usual preprocessing for comparison across scales.

tools.name: Quantile
tools.description: Gives the q-th quantile of a list or distribution, with a parameter specification controlling which of the standard interpolation definitions is used. Quantile[list, {q1, q2, ...}] returns several quantiles at once. It is the general order-statistic accessor behind Median and Quartiles.
tools.usage:
Quantile[list, q]
Quantile[list, {q1, q2, ...}]
Quantile[dist, q]
Quantile[list, q, {{a, b}, {c, d}}]
tools.example:
Quantile[Range[100], 0.9]
Quantile[data, {0.05, 0.5, 0.95}]
Quantile[NormalDistribution[0, 1], 0.975]
Quantile[Range[10], 1/2]
tools.notes: The default definition for lists picks an actual data value; supply the parameter specification {{0, 0}, {1, 0}} to match the linear-interpolation convention used by many other systems.

tools.name: Quartiles
tools.description: Gives {lower quartile, median, upper quartile} for a list or distribution in one call. InterquartileRange gives the difference between the outer two, which is the robust spread measure used in box plots. Both are shortcuts over Quantile with the standard quartile definition.
tools.example:
Quartiles[Range[100]]
Quartiles[NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
InterquartileRange[data]
QuartileDeviation[data]

tools.name: Correlation
tools.description: Gives the Pearson correlation coefficient between two vectors, or the correlation matrix of the columns of a data matrix. Values range from -1 to 1 and measure linear association only. SpearmanRho and KendallTau provide rank-based alternatives that capture monotone but nonlinear relationships.
tools.example:
Correlation[{1, 2, 3, 4}, {2, 4, 6, 8.1}]
Correlation[Transpose[{xs, ys}]]
Correlation[data] // MatrixForm
SpearmanRho[xs, ys]
tools.notes: Correlation[matrix] treats each column as a variable, so transpose your data if observations are in columns.

tools.name: Covariance
tools.description: Gives the covariance between two vectors or the covariance matrix of the columns of a data matrix, using the unbiased n-1 divisor. It is the unnormalized version of Correlation and carries the product of the two variables' units. For a distribution it gives the exact symbolic covariance.
tools.example:
Covariance[{1, 2, 3}, {2, 4, 7}]
Covariance[Transpose[{xs, ys}]] // MatrixForm
Covariance[MultinormalDistribution[{0, 0}, {{1, 0.5}, {0.5, 2}}]]
CholeskyDecomposition[Covariance[data]]

tools.name: Moment
tools.description: Gives the r-th raw moment of a list or distribution, i.e. the expectation of x^r. CentralMoment gives the moment about the mean and FactorialMoment the factorial moment. These are the building blocks of Skewness, Kurtosis and the method of moments.
tools.usage:
Moment[list, r]
Moment[dist, r]
CentralMoment[list, r]
tools.example:
Moment[{1, 2, 3, 4}, 2]
Moment[NormalDistribution[0, 1], 4]
CentralMoment[data, 3]
Moment[PoissonDistribution[lambda], 2]

tools.name: CentralMoment
tools.description: Gives the r-th moment about the mean of a list or distribution. The second central moment is the population variance, and the third and fourth underlie Skewness and Kurtosis. Cumulant gives the related cumulants, which are additive for independent variables.
tools.usage:
CentralMoment[list, r]
CentralMoment[dist, r]
Cumulant[dist, r]
tools.example:
CentralMoment[{1, 2, 3, 4}, 2]
CentralMoment[NormalDistribution[mu, sigma], 4]
Cumulant[PoissonDistribution[lambda], 3]
CentralMoment[data, 3]/StandardDeviation[data]^3

tools.name: Skewness
tools.description: Measures the asymmetry of a distribution or dataset, positive for a long right tail and zero for any symmetric distribution. It is the standardized third central moment. Large sample skewness is a common diagnostic for deciding whether to transform data before applying normal-theory methods.
tools.example:
Skewness[{1, 2, 3, 10}]
Skewness[NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
Skewness[ExponentialDistribution[1]]
Skewness[RandomVariate[LogNormalDistribution[0, 1], 10000]]

tools.name: Kurtosis
tools.description: Measures the tail weight of a distribution or dataset, with the value 3 for a normal distribution in the convention Wolfram Language uses. Values above 3 indicate heavier tails and more outliers than the normal. QuantileDeviation and robust alternatives are less sensitive to extreme values.
tools.example:
Kurtosis[NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
Kurtosis[{1, 2, 3, 4, 100}]
Kurtosis[StudentTDistribution[5]]
Kurtosis[data] - 3
tools.notes: Wolfram Language reports raw kurtosis, not excess kurtosis; subtract 3 to compare with software that reports the excess.

tools.name: RandomReal
tools.description: Generates pseudorandom real numbers uniformly distributed in a range, with a dimensions argument producing arrays of any shape. RandomReal[] alone gives one number in [0, 1]. WorkingPrecision produces arbitrary-precision random values, and the results are packed arrays for speed.
tools.usage:
RandomReal[]
RandomReal[max]
RandomReal[{min, max}]
RandomReal[range, n]
RandomReal[range, {m, n}]
tools.example:
RandomReal[]
RandomReal[{-1, 1}, 10]
RandomReal[1, {3, 3}]
RandomReal[{0, 2 Pi}, 5]
RandomReal[1, 5, WorkingPrecision -> 30]
tools.notes: For non-uniform distributions use RandomVariate with an explicit distribution rather than transforming uniform numbers by hand.

tools.name: RandomInteger
tools.description: Generates pseudorandom integers uniformly in a range, inclusive of both endpoints. RandomInteger[] gives 0 or 1, RandomInteger[n] gives 0 through n, and a {min, max} range with a dimensions argument produces arrays. It also accepts a distribution as the first argument for non-uniform integers.
tools.usage:
RandomInteger[]
RandomInteger[max]
RandomInteger[{min, max}]
RandomInteger[range, n]
RandomInteger[dist, n]
tools.example:
RandomInteger[]
RandomInteger[10]
RandomInteger[{1, 6}, 10]
RandomInteger[1, {4, 4}]
RandomInteger[BinomialDistribution[10, 0.5], 5]

tools.name: RandomVariate
tools.description: Generates pseudorandom values from any symbolic probability distribution, including derived, mixture, transformed and empirical distributions. A dimensions argument produces arrays of samples efficiently. It is the general sampling function and the foundation of Monte Carlo work in the Wolfram Language.
tools.example:
RandomVariate[NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
RandomVariate[NormalDistribution[100, 15], 1000]
RandomVariate[PoissonDistribution[3], {5, 5}]
RandomVariate[MultinormalDistribution[{0, 0}, {{1, 0.5}, {0.5, 1}}], 100]
Histogram[RandomVariate[ExponentialDistribution[1], 10000]]

tools.name: RandomChoice
tools.description: Chooses elements at random from a list, with replacement, optionally with specified weights. RandomChoice[{w1, w2} -> {e1, e2}, n] draws with the given relative probabilities. It is the tool for bootstrap resampling, weighted sampling and simple simulation.
tools.usage:
RandomChoice[list]
RandomChoice[list, n]
RandomChoice[weights -> list, n]
RandomChoice[list, {m, n}]
tools.example:
RandomChoice[{a, b, c}]
RandomChoice[{1, 2, 3}, 10]
RandomChoice[{0.7, 0.3} -> {"heads", "tails"}, 20]
RandomChoice[data, Length[data]]
RandomChoice[{H, T}, {5, 5}]
tools.notes: RandomChoice samples with replacement; use RandomSample when elements must not repeat.

tools.name: RandomSample
tools.description: Chooses elements at random without replacement, so no element appears twice. RandomSample[list] with no count returns a random permutation of the whole list. Weights can be supplied for probability-proportional-to-size sampling without replacement.
tools.usage:
RandomSample[list]
RandomSample[list, n]
RandomSample[weights -> list, n]
RandomSample[n]
tools.example:
RandomSample[{a, b, c, d}]
RandomSample[Range[100], 10]
RandomSample[{1, 2, 3, 4} -> {a, b, c, d}, 2]
RandomSample[5]
train = RandomSample[data, Round[0.8 Length[data]]];

tools.name: SeedRandom
tools.description: Sets the seed of the pseudorandom generator so that a sequence of random results can be reproduced exactly. SeedRandom[] with no argument seeds from the clock. Wrapping code in BlockRandom isolates its random state so it does not disturb the surrounding stream.
tools.notes: Always seed explicitly in scripts whose results must be reproducible, and record the seed alongside the results.

tools.name: NormalDistribution
tools.description: The normal (Gaussian) distribution with given mean and standard deviation, defaulting to the standard normal when called with no arguments. It works symbolically with PDF, CDF, Mean, Variance, Expectation and RandomVariate. MultinormalDistribution is the multivariate version, parametrized by a mean vector and covariance matrix.
tools.example:
PDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], x]
CDF[NormalDistribution[100, 15], 130]
RandomVariate[NormalDistribution[0, 1], 5]
Mean[NormalDistribution[mu, sigma]]
Quantile[NormalDistribution[0, 1], 0.975]

tools.name: UniformDistribution
tools.description: The continuous uniform distribution over an interval, defaulting to [0, 1], with a list of intervals giving the multivariate version over a box. DiscreteUniformDistribution covers the equiprobable integer case. It is the base distribution for many sampling and simulation constructions.
tools.usage:
UniformDistribution[]
UniformDistribution[{min, max}]
UniformDistribution[{{a1, b1}, {a2, b2}}]
DiscreteUniformDistribution[{min, max}]
tools.example:
PDF[UniformDistribution[{0, 2}], x]
Mean[UniformDistribution[{a, b}]]
RandomVariate[UniformDistribution[{-1, 1}], 5]
RandomVariate[DiscreteUniformDistribution[{1, 6}], 10]

tools.name: BinomialDistribution
tools.description: The distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials each with probability p. It is discrete, so PDF gives the probability mass function. BernoulliDistribution is the single-trial case and MultinomialDistribution the many-category generalization.
tools.example:
PDF[BinomialDistribution[10, 0.5], 5]
CDF[BinomialDistribution[20, 0.1], 3]
Mean[BinomialDistribution[n, p]]
RandomVariate[BinomialDistribution[100, 0.3], 10]
Probability[x > 7, x \[Distributed] BinomialDistribution[10, 0.5]]

tools.name: PoissonDistribution
tools.description: The distribution of the number of events in a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate lambda. Its mean and variance are both lambda. It is the limit of the binomial distribution for many trials with small success probability, and is paired with the exponential distribution for waiting times.
tools.example:
PDF[PoissonDistribution[3], 2]
CDF[PoissonDistribution[3], 5]
Mean[PoissonDistribution[lambda]]
Variance[PoissonDistribution[lambda]]
RandomVariate[PoissonDistribution[4.5], 20]

tools.name: ExponentialDistribution
tools.description: The continuous distribution of waiting times between events in a Poisson process, with rate parameter lambda and mean 1/lambda. It is the unique continuous distribution with the memoryless property. GammaDistribution and WeibullDistribution generalize it for reliability modelling.
tools.example:
PDF[ExponentialDistribution[2], x]
Mean[ExponentialDistribution[lambda]]
CDF[ExponentialDistribution[0.5], 3]
RandomVariate[ExponentialDistribution[1], 1000]
SurvivalFunction[ExponentialDistribution[lambda], t]

tools.name: StudentTDistribution
tools.description: The Student t distribution with nu degrees of freedom, heavier tailed than the normal and approaching it as nu grows. It is the sampling distribution of a standardized mean when the variance is estimated from the data, which is why it underlies the t test and confidence intervals. ChiSquareDistribution and FRatioDistribution complete the classical trio of sampling distributions.
tools.usage:
StudentTDistribution[nu]
StudentTDistribution[mu, sigma, nu]
ChiSquareDistribution[nu]
FRatioDistribution[n, m]
tools.example:
PDF[StudentTDistribution[5], x]
Quantile[StudentTDistribution[10], 0.975]
Variance[StudentTDistribution[nu]]
CDF[ChiSquareDistribution[3], 7.8]
Quantile[FRatioDistribution[3, 20], 0.95]

tools.name: PDF
tools.description: Gives the probability density function of a continuous distribution or the probability mass function of a discrete one, as a symbolic expression in the variable. PDF[dist, x] can be plotted, integrated and differentiated like any other expression. For multivariate distributions the variable is a list.
tools.example:
PDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], x]
PDF[BinomialDistribution[10, 0.5], 3]
Plot[PDF[ExponentialDistribution[1], x], {x, 0, 5}]
Integrate[PDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], x], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]
PDF[MultinormalDistribution[{0, 0}, IdentityMatrix[2]], {x, y}]

tools.name: CDF
tools.description: Gives the cumulative distribution function, the probability that a random value is at most x. It returns a symbolic expression for parametric distributions and an exact step function for empirical ones. SurvivalFunction gives the complement, which is numerically better in the far right tail.
tools.example:
CDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], 1.96]
CDF[PoissonDistribution[3], 5]
Plot[CDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], x], {x, -4, 4}]
SurvivalFunction[ExponentialDistribution[1], 10]
CDF[NormalDistribution[mu, sigma], x]

tools.name: InverseCDF
tools.description: Gives the quantile function, the value x for which the CDF equals a given probability. It is used to compute critical values for hypothesis tests and confidence intervals, and to generate variates by inverse transform sampling. For discrete distributions it returns the smallest value whose CDF reaches the target.
tools.example:
InverseCDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], 0.975]
InverseCDF[StudentTDistribution[10], 0.95]
InverseCDF[ChiSquareDistribution[3], 0.99]
InverseCDF[NormalDistribution[0, 1], RandomReal[1, 5]]
InverseCDF[BinomialDistribution[10, 0.5], 0.5]
tools.notes: Quantile[dist, q] gives the same result and is the more common spelling when working with data and distributions together.

tools.name: Expectation
tools.description: Computes the exact symbolic expected value of an expression with respect to one or more random variables, written with the \[Distributed] operator. It handles conditional expectations with the Assumptions option and works for discrete, continuous and multivariate distributions. NExpectation computes the same thing numerically when no closed form exists.
tools.usage:
Expectation[expr, x \[Distributed] dist]
Expectation[expr, {x \[Distributed] d1, y \[Distributed] d2}]
Expectation[expr, x \[Distributed] dist, Assumptions -> cond]
tools.example:
Expectation[x^2, x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
Expectation[x, x \[Distributed] PoissonDistribution[lambda]]
Expectation[x y, {x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1], y \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]}]
Expectation[Max[x, 0], x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[mu, sigma]]

tools.name: NExpectation
tools.description: Computes expected values numerically by quadrature or summation, for cases where Expectation cannot find a closed form. It accepts the same \[Distributed] syntax and takes NIntegrate-style method and precision options. It is the practical choice for complicated payoff functions and empirical distributions.
tools.usage:
NExpectation[expr, x \[Distributed] dist]
NExpectation[expr, x \[Distributed] dist, Method -> m]
tools.example:
NExpectation[Sin[x]^2, x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
NExpectation[Max[x - 100, 0], x \[Distributed] LogNormalDistribution[4.6, 0.3]]
NExpectation[x^3, x \[Distributed] BetaDistribution[2, 5]]

tools.name: Probability
tools.description: Computes the exact probability that a logical condition holds for random variables with specified distributions. Conditions can involve inequalities, logical combinations and several variables at once. NProbability is the numerical counterpart for cases without a closed form.
tools.usage:
Probability[cond, x \[Distributed] dist]
Probability[cond, {x \[Distributed] d1, y \[Distributed] d2}]
NProbability[cond, x \[Distributed] dist]
tools.example:
Probability[x > 1, x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
Probability[x + y < 1, {x \[Distributed] UniformDistribution[], y \[Distributed] UniformDistribution[]}]
Probability[x > 7, x \[Distributed] BinomialDistribution[10, 0.5]]
NProbability[Sin[x] > 0.5, x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 2]]

tools.name: EmpiricalDistribution
tools.description: Builds a discrete distribution directly from data, placing equal probability on each observed value, or weighted probabilities when weights are supplied. The result behaves like any other distribution, so PDF, CDF, Quantile, Mean and RandomVariate all work, which makes bootstrap resampling a one-liner. SmoothKernelDistribution gives a continuous kernel-density version.

tools.name: TransformedDistribution
tools.description: Gives the exact distribution of a function of one or more random variables, deriving the new density symbolically. It handles sums, products, ratios, maxima and arbitrary smooth transformations, which makes analytic derivations that would otherwise be laborious immediate. ParameterMixtureDistribution and ProductDistribution cover related constructions.
tools.usage:
TransformedDistribution[expr, x \[Distributed] dist]
TransformedDistribution[expr, {x \[Distributed] d1, y \[Distributed] d2}]
ProductDistribution[d1, d2]
tools.example:
TransformedDistribution[x^2, x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]]
TransformedDistribution[x + y, {x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1], y \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]}]
PDF[TransformedDistribution[Exp[x], x \[Distributed] NormalDistribution[0, 1]], y]
TransformedDistribution[Max[x, y], {x \[Distributed] UniformDistribution[], y \[Distributed] UniformDistribution[]}]

tools.name: EstimatedDistribution
tools.description: Fits the parameters of a specified distribution family to data, by maximum likelihood or another chosen method. The result is a distribution object with numeric parameters that can be used exactly like a parametric distribution. ParameterEstimator selects between maximum likelihood, method of moments and other estimators.
tools.example:
EstimatedDistribution[data, NormalDistribution[mu, sigma]]
EstimatedDistribution[RandomVariate[ExponentialDistribution[2], 500], ExponentialDistribution[lambda]]
EstimatedDistribution[data, WeibullDistribution[a, b], ParameterEstimator -> "MaximumLikelihood"]
Mean[EstimatedDistribution[data, GammaDistribution[a, b]]]

tools.name: FindDistribution
tools.description: Automatically searches a library of distribution families and returns the one that best fits the data, optionally returning the top several candidates with their scores. TargetFunctions restricts the search to a chosen set of families. It is a quick exploratory tool rather than a substitute for a considered model choice.
tools.usage:
FindDistribution[data]
FindDistribution[data, n]
FindDistribution[data, n, TargetFunctions -> {d1, d2}]
tools.example:
FindDistribution[RandomVariate[ExponentialDistribution[2], 500]]
FindDistribution[data, 3]
FindDistribution[data, 2, TargetFunctions -> {NormalDistribution, GammaDistribution}]
FindDistribution[data, 1, "Score"]
tools.notes: Always confirm a suggested fit with DistributionFitTest and a visual check such as a quantile plot before relying on it.

tools.name: DistributionFitTest
tools.description: Tests the null hypothesis that data was drawn from a specified distribution, returning a p-value or a full HypothesisTestData object. Requesting "TestDataTable" or a specific test name gives the Anderson-Darling, Cramer-von Mises, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Pearson chi-square and other statistics. With no distribution specified it tests for normality.
tools.usage:
DistributionFitTest[data]
DistributionFitTest[data, dist]
DistributionFitTest[data, dist, "property"]
DistributionFitTest[data, dist, "TestDataTable"]
tools.example:
DistributionFitTest[RandomVariate[NormalDistribution[], 100]]
DistributionFitTest[data, ExponentialDistribution[1]]
DistributionFitTest[data, Automatic, "TestDataTable"]
DistributionFitTest[data, NormalDistribution[0, 1], "PValue", "AndersonDarling"]
tools.notes: A large p-value does not prove the distribution is correct, only that the data does not contradict it; large samples reject almost any parametric model.

tools.name: TTest
tools.description: Performs a Student t test of whether the mean of a dataset differs from a specified value, or whether the means of two datasets differ. It returns a p-value by default and a full HypothesisTestData object when properties are requested. Options select a one- or two-sided alternative and paired versus unpaired comparison.
tools.usage:
TTest[data]
TTest[data, mu0]
TTest[{data1, data2}]
TTest[data, mu0, "property"]
tools.example:
TTest[RandomVariate[NormalDistribution[0.2, 1], 50]]
TTest[data, 100]
TTest[{groupA, groupB}]
TTest[data, 0, "TestDataTable"]
TTest[{before, after}, 0, AlternativeHypothesis -> "Greater"]
tools.notes: TTest assumes approximate normality; LocationTest chooses an appropriate test automatically and LocationEquivalenceTest compares more than two groups.

tools.name: LocationTest
tools.description: Tests hypotheses about the location (mean or median) of one or two datasets, automatically choosing among the t test, Mann-Whitney, sign test and others based on the data's properties. Naming a specific test forces that choice. It is the recommended general entry point for location inference because it handles the assumption checking for you.
tools.usage:
LocationTest[data]
LocationTest[data, mu0]
LocationTest[{data1, data2}]
LocationTest[data, mu0, "property"]
LocationTest[data, mu0, "TestDataTable", "MannWhitney"]
tools.example:
LocationTest[data]
LocationTest[{groupA, groupB}]
LocationTest[data, 0, "TestDataTable"]
LocationTest[{x, y}, 0, "PValue", "MannWhitney"]
LocationEquivalenceTest[{g1, g2, g3}]
tools.notes: Companion functions include VarianceTest and VarianceEquivalenceTest for spread, and IndependenceTest and PearsonChiSquareTest for association.
